design_detail: Narrative review in Current Epidemiology Reports (2019; Topical Collection on Injury Epidemiology) by six authors: four from the University of Kentucky (biostatistics, the Kentucky Injury Prevention and Research Center, pharmacy practice and science, preventive medicine and environmental health, health management and policy), one from the University of Pittsburgh (biostatistics) and one from the University of Florida (Department of Pathology, Immunology and Laboratory Medicine: Goldberger, a co-chair of the 2013 SAMHSA consensus panel according to that statement's Appendix A, card sc_goldberger_2013, a role this review does not state). It describes how US drug overdose deaths are investigated by medical examiners and coroners, certified, transmitted by state vital-statistics offices and coded to ICD-10 by NCHS (with a flowchart, Fig. 1), then the analytic problems this creates (unspecified drugs, abrupt changes in specification or testing, variation in undetermined intent, delays, the changing meaning of 'prescription opioid' codes once illicit fentanyl arrived), and the tools proposed to correct them (cause-of-death text analysis, statistical reallocation of unspecified deaths, toxicology markers, enhanced multi-source surveillance). No search strategy or selection criteria; 95 references, 11 marked as of major importance in the text citations (the reference list prints the mark beside 5 of them), 12 written by the review's own authors (4 of the 11). Filed as narrative-review with the editors' checklist.
can_establish: How the US system that produces drug-overdose death counts works and where, according to the authors and the sources they cite, it loses or distorts information on which drugs were involved; which correction methods had been proposed by 2019 and what they estimated.
cannot_establish: The size of any undercount or misattribution as a pooled or appraised estimate (no search, appraisal or synthesis; the estimates are relayed from single studies, several by the authors), or how far deaths are wrongly attributed to opioids, which the review barely addresses.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Sources chosen by the authors: peer-reviewed studies, position and consensus papers (NAME, SAMHSA, OSAC), NCHS and CDC reports and data (CDC WONDER), federal survey and policy reports, and one personal communication.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors' own and centred on US opioid deaths. Several key empirical statements come from the authors' own work: the CSTE commentary (Slavova et al., 2015), the SAMHSA panel (Goldberger et al., 2013), the reallocation estimate (Buchanich et al., 2018), and Kentucky studies on benzodiazepine listing, gabapentin testing and enhanced surveillance. The over-attribution side (deaths wrongly put down to opioids) is hardly represented.

exposure.measurement: Not a study. The review describes drug involvement as recorded on certificates (Part I causes; contributing conditions) and coded by NCHS to ICD-10 multiple-cause T codes, and the post-mortem toxicology that underlies it, for which the authors say the US has no nationally accepted best practices, standards or guidelines (The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 6th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: The review sets the recommendation that drugs not contributing to death be left off the certificate beside Gill's statement that, because a single drug's role can rarely be separated in multi-drug intoxications, it is customary to list all drugs above trace amounts (7th paragraph of that subsection), without reconciling them. It reports a Kentucky study (by the authors' group) in which benzodiazepines were less often listed as contributing drugs than fentanyl, heroin, methadone or cocaine (Enhanced Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 3rd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable; the review discusses ICD-10 underlying-cause and multiple-cause codes, cause-of-death text analysis, toxicology markers (6-acetylmorphine, morphine-to-codeine ratio, 4-ANPP, norfentanyl) and adjusted rates from cited studies.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not assessed; the authors note that the assumptions behind the statistical adjustments are reasonable but difficult to verify.
outcomes.operationalization: Overdose death = ICD-10 underlying cause X40 to X44, X60 to X64, X85 or Y10 to Y14; drug involvement = T36 to T50 multiple-cause codes; a death whose only drug code is T50.9 typically had no drug or drug class written on the certificate (Death Certificate ICD-10 Coding, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).

analysis.effect_sizes: No synthesis. Figures relayed from cited sources: certificates listing specific drugs, by investigation system, centralized medical examiner 92%, decentralized medical examiner 71%, hybrid 73%, coroner 62% (Warner et al., 2013); South Carolina's prescription-opioid (T40.2 to T40.4) rate 4.7 per 100,000 in 2013 and 9.3 in 2014 while specificity rose from 57.7% to 94.4%; Kentucky gabapentin prevalence among overdose decedents 2.9% (2013) to 17% (2014) after routine testing began; undetermined intent 85% of poisoning deaths in Maryland and over 40% in Utah against 8% nationally (Warner et al., 2013), and in 2016 from 1% (Connecticut, Massachusetts) to 68% (Maryland); T40.4 as a share of T40.2 to T40.4 deaths in 2016 under 20% in Nevada and Utah and over 80% in New Hampshire and Massachusetts; about 70,000 unintentional opioid-related deaths possibly unaccounted for in 1999 to 2015 (Buchanich et al., 2018); 2015 opioid-involved rate 12.46 per 100,000 after adjustment against 10.31 reported, 21% higher (Ruhm, 2018); benzodiazepines listed as contributing on certificates in 67% (alprazolam) and under 40% (clonazepam, diazepam), against fentanyl 89%, heroin 88%, methadone 81%, cocaine 77% (Kentucky; denominator not stated in the review); certificates naming specific drugs or classes 75% (2011) to 85% (2016) (Hedegaard et al.); 75% of medical examiner and coroner offices always requesting testing for opioids other than heroin or fentanyl and 51% to 75% always requesting testing for fentanyl and heroin (2017 NFLIS survey); 32% of offices with computerized, networked systems (2017 survey).
analysis.selective_reporting: The review gives the undercounting side in detail and the over-attribution side (incidental drugs listed, attribution without lethal concentrations, post-mortem interpretation) almost none. The statement that about 20% of overdose certificates name no specific drug is given without a source.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A descriptive account of how US overdose death data are produced, with relayed evidence that drug specificity on certificates varies by jurisdiction and over time, that changes in recording or testing practice can produce artefactual jumps (South Carolina 2014; Kentucky gabapentin 2014), that intent coding varies widely, that some drugs are less often listed than others when detected, and that statistical reallocation suggests opioid involvement was undercounted (about 70,000 deaths in 1999 to 2015; 21% in 2015).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusions stay close to this: certificates are the foundation of surveillance, variation in certification can bias rates, text analysis improves specific-drug quantification, enhanced surveillance has potential, and uniform national standards are unlikely soon in a fragmented system. Gaps: (1) the abstract says text analysis tools improve quantification of specific opioid rates, while the body says they cannot reach the roughly 20% of certificates naming no specific drug; (2) the reallocation and adjusted-rate estimates are relayed with only a one-sentence caveat (assumptions reasonable but difficult to verify), one of them from a co-author; (3) a morphine-to-codeine ratio above 1 is presented as a strong and probable indicator of heroin from cited studies without appraisal; (4) the South Carolina explanation rests on personal correspondence; (5) the framing is one-directional (undercounting), with no discussion of how often listed drugs did not contribute, although the review itself reports the custom of listing every drug above trace amounts.

timeline.event: Warner et al., state variation in certifying manner of death and the drugs involved (Academic Forensic Pathology), source of the system-type and undetermined-intent figures; not indexed in PubMed according to the project's list.
SAMHSA consensus panel definitions, one of the three recommendation papers the review names (card sc_goldberger_2013, this reader).
CSTE Overdose Subcommittee commentary on jurisdiction variation in naming drugs, by the first author (card sc_slavova_2015, this reader).
Buchanich et al. reallocation of unspecified unintentional overdose deaths, 1999 to 2015 (co-author's study; read by another reader in this round).
Ruhm, corrected US opioid-involved poisoning deaths and rates, 1999 to 2015 (cited as ref 57).
Horon et al., standard death certificates against enhanced surveillance for heroin overdose deaths (cited as ref 82; read by another reader in this round).

NCHS report: overdose certificates with a drug or drug-class code rose to 96.0% by 2023 from 87.7% in 2017 (card sc_garnett_2026, this reader), continuing the 75% (2011) to 85% (2016) series this review quotes.

replication.where_it_stands: A 2019 map of the problems, still useful as an orientation and as a pointer to primary studies. Its figures should be cited from the primary sources after they are read. National specificity has since improved further (96.0% with a drug or drug-class code in 2023, Garnett et al., 2026), so the 'about 20% unspecified' figure is out of date; the questions it raises about jurisdictional variation, testing practice and intent coding are addressed by later studies on the project's list.

funding.declared_conflicts: Svetla Slavova, Chris Delcher, Jeannine M. Buchanich, Terry L. Bunn, Julia F. Costich and Bruce A. Goldberger each declare no potential conflicts of interest (Compliance with Ethical Standards › Conflict of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Four of the six authors are at the University of Kentucky (Slavova, Delcher, Bunn and Costich; Slavova, Bunn and Costich also at the Kentucky Injury Prevention and Research Center, and the Kentucky enhanced surveillance the review describes is reported by Hargrove et al., with Bunn and Slavova among its authors), one at the University of Pittsburgh (Buchanich) and one at the University of Florida (Goldberger). Authors' own studies supply several of the review's key figures and four of its eleven references of major importance. NCHS staff (Warner, Hedegaard, Braun) are thanked for comments and for help with the flowchart. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the undercount: link a national sample of overdose deaths, including those coded only T50.9 or T40.6, to full toxicology and medical examiner or coroner files and measure drug-specific omission by jurisdiction and system type. For the other direction, which the review leaves open: in the same linked sample, have independent forensic reviewers judge which listed drugs contributed, and measure how often drugs on certificates were incidental.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; 95 references chosen by the authors.

No formal appraisal; a few limitations are named (the adjustment assumptions are difficult to verify), but survey figures, the heroin ratio and the NAME recommendations (called evidence-based) are relayed without appraisal.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 12 of 95 references and 4 of the 11 flagged as of major importance are by the review's authors, including the reallocation estimate, the benzodiazepine-listing and gabapentin-testing findings, and one of the three recommendation papers the review names (the SAMHSA panel, co-chaired by a co-author).

Most statements are attributed and hedged, but the 'about 20% unspecified' figure is unsourced and sits awkwardly with the 85% (2016) specificity figure quoted later, and the South Carolina explanation rests on personal correspondence.

domains.domain: Balance of attention to undercounting and to over-attribution of deaths to opioids
domains.note: Under-represented: over-attribution. Undercounting is covered in depth; the other direction appears only in relayed recommendations, none quantified: the SAMHSA panel's distinction between drug-caused and drug-detected deaths (MDI subsection, 4th paragraph), the rule that non-contributing drugs be left off the certificate beside Gill's remark on listing all drugs above trace amounts (7th paragraph), and NAME's call to interpret toxicology in the context of the circumstances (3rd paragraph).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review; the editors' checklist is used, with the overall judgment no milder than the worst domain (no systematic search). The review is careful and well sourced as orientation, and most statements are attributed, but it pools and appraises nothing, relies in part on the authors' own work, and covers mainly one direction of error. It may be cited for the description of the US investigation, certification and coding pathway (who certifies, who codes, which codes), for the named sources of distortion (unspecified certificates, abrupt changes in specification or testing, variation in undetermined intent, delays, the T40.4 problem once illicit fentanyl spread), and as a pointer to primary studies. Its numbers (system-type percentages, South Carolina, Kentucky gabapentin, 70,000 uncounted deaths, 21% adjustment, benzodiazepine listing, survey shares) are second-hand and should be cited from the primary sources once read; the claim stays at draft if it rests on this review alone (METHODS §5.3).

key_findings.finding: Overdose mortality data are produced by several agencies and actors, with no single agency having quality-control oversight of the whole process (investigation, certification, registration, coding, surveillance; Fig. 1).
key_findings.note: Fig. 1 is a flowchart image; its legend was read, the image itself was not viewed (the browser pane was hidden, and a screenshot taken earlier in this session came back blank).

key_findings.finding: Who decides: medicolegal death investigations are opened under state law for unexplained, sudden or unnatural deaths, including suspected overdoses; the officers are medical examiners or coroners, who vary in how they are selected (appointed or elected) and in professional credentials, and who complete the medical part of the certificate (underlying cause, causal chain, other significant conditions, manner).
key_findings.locator: Investigation and Classification of Overdose Deaths › The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Toxicology: the authors state that the US has no nationally accepted best practices, standards or guidelines for post-mortem toxicology and that many jurisdictions do not test all suspected overdose deaths for novel substances including fentanyl and its analogues; a 2017 national survey of offices reported that only 75% always request testing for opioids other than heroin or fentanyl and only 51% to 75% always request testing for fentanyl and heroin.
key_findings.locator: The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand (NFLIS 2017 medical examiner/coroner office survey, ref 34); the survey's response rate is not given.

key_findings.finding: Listing drugs: drugs physiologically significant in causing death should be listed individually, preferably by generic name, in Part I, and drugs that did not contribute should not be recorded; the review also quotes Gill that in multi-drug intoxications a single drug's role can usually not be separated, so it is customary to list every drug found above trace amounts.
key_findings.locator: The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Who codes: after filing with the state office of vital statistics, a limited set of fields is sent to NCHS, which codes the cause-of-death text to ICD-10: one underlying cause and up to 20 contributing-cause codes. Phrases such as overdose of drug, toxic effect, intoxication, drug taken inadvertently, lethal amount, wrong drug given in error or wrong dose taken accidentally are coded as drug poisoning even in treatment settings; the underlying cause falls in X40 to X44, X60 to X64, X85 or Y10 to Y14, with T36 to T50 codes for drugs.
key_findings.locator: Investigation and Classification of Overdose Deaths › Death Certificate ICD-10 Coding, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Opioid codes are broad: T40.0 opium, T40.1 heroin, T40.2 other opioids (oxycodone, codeine, hydrocodone, oxymorphone and morphine together), T40.3 methadone, T40.4 other synthetic narcotics, T40.6 other and unspecified narcotics ('opioid', 'opiate'); a death whose only drug code is T50.9 typically had no drug or drug class written on the certificate.

Quoted from Warner et al. (2013): states with centralized medical examiner systems averaged 92% completeness in listing drugs, against decentralized medical examiner 71%, hybrid 73% and coroner 62% systems; 85% of poisoning deaths in Maryland and over 40% in Utah were classed as undetermined intent against 8% nationally. In 2016 the undetermined share still ranged from 1% (Connecticut, Massachusetts) to 68% (Maryland).
key_findings.locator: Epidemiologic Analysis of Drug Overdose Death Data › Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 1st and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Artefactual jumps: South Carolina's age-adjusted prescription-opioid (T40.2 to T40.4) death rate went from 4.7 per 100,000 in 2013 to 9.3 in 2014, mainly because the share of drug-poisoning certificates listing specific drugs rose from 57.7% to 94.4% after the state vital-statistics office began collecting drug names for all deaths in January 2014; routine gabapentin testing in Kentucky from July 2014 raised gabapentin prevalence among overdose decedents from 2.9% to 17%. The authors warn that gradual procedural improvements produce smaller, harder-to-detect shifts.
key_findings.locator: Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The South Carolina explanation is from personal correspondence with the state office.

key_findings.finding: Delays and provisional undercounting: ICD-10 R99 (unspecified causes) is used as the underlying cause for injury deaths until investigation ends, and an NCHS study found an inverse relationship between the share coded R99 and the share coded drug poisoning; the lag to certificate availability is much longer for overdose deaths than for natural deaths or suicides, usually because of toxicology delays.
key_findings.locator: Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 5th paragraph; Statistical Adjustment for Undercounting, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The meaning of 'prescription opioid' codes changed with illicit fentanyl: CDC had used T40.2 to T40.4, and Seth et al. proposed dropping T40.4 because synthetic-opioid deaths were likely due to illicitly made fentanyl; in 2016 T40.4 made up under 20% of T40.2 to T40.4 deaths in Nevada and Utah but over 80% in New Hampshire and Massachusetts.
key_findings.locator: Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 6th and 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Text analysis of certificates can identify specific opioids that ICD-10 groups together (an NCHS and FDA tool), but cannot help for the approximately 20% of overdose certificates that name no specific drug.
key_findings.locator: Identifying Specific Opioids by Cause-of-Death Text Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: No source is given for the 20%; the review later quotes NCHS figures of 85% specified in 2016.

key_findings.finding: Statistical correction: Buchanich et al. reallocated unspecified unintentional overdose deaths in proportion to opioid involvement among specified deaths, by state and year, and estimated about 70,000 unintentional opioid-related deaths unaccounted for in 1999 to 2015; Ruhm's model-based adjustment gave a 2015 opioid-involved rate of 12.46 per 100,000 against 10.31 reported (21% higher). Ruhm's adjusted state rates for 2008 to 2014 differed from reported rates by widely varying percentages that reflected each state's share of unspecified deaths. The authors call the assumptions reasonable but difficult to verify, and add that models could include characteristics of the investigation systems (jurisdiction type, toxicology protocols), but such information is not readily available.
key_findings.locator: Statistical Adjustment for Undercounting, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand; Buchanich is a co-author of this review.

key_findings.finding: Toxicology markers proposed for enhanced surveillance: heroin's specific metabolite 6-acetylmorphine is often undetected because of rapid metabolism to morphine; cited studies treat a morphine-to-codeine concentration ratio above 1 as a strong and probable indicator of heroin; 4-ANPP indicates illicitly made fentanyl or analogues; heroin metabolites can proxy a short survival time, and absent norfentanyl may indicate rapid death after fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Enhanced Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Drugs found but not listed: in a Kentucky study (the authors' group) that linked certificates with post-mortem toxicology, benzodiazepines were less often listed as contributing drugs on certificates, 67% for alprazolam and under 40% for clonazepam and diazepam, against fentanyl 89%, heroin 88%, methadone 81% and cocaine 77% (the review does not state the denominator, presumably decedents in whom each drug was detected); in a multi-jurisdiction study, the region with the lowest gabapentin prevalence was the only one not testing every potential overdose for gabapentin. The authors recommend reporting the type of toxicology testing (screening or confirmatory; routine or on request).
key_findings.locator: Enhanced Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: That the Kentucky study linked certificates with post-mortem toxicology is taken from the title of reference 62, not from the review's sentence.

key_findings.finding: Enhanced surveillance: CDC funded 32 states in 2016 to 2017 for Enhanced State Opioid Overdose Surveillance, with at least 60% of the September 2017 supplemental funding mandated for medical examiners and coroners, including comprehensive toxicology; its reporting system (SUDORS) covers only unintentional opioid overdose deaths.
key_findings.locator: Enhanced Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Specificity trend and capacity: NCHS reported that overdose certificates identifying specific drugs or drug classes rose every year, 75% (2011), 76%, 78%, 81%, 83%, 85% (2016); a 2017 survey found only 32% of responding medical examiner and coroner offices had computerized, networked systems. The authors conclude that the fragmented system makes uniform national standards unlikely in the near future.
key_findings.locator: Death Certificates Remain the Core of Population-Based Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Conclusions

key_findings.finding: Three papers set out recommendations for certifying opioid-related deaths, as the review relays them: the National Association of Medical Examiners position paper, which the review calls evidence-based (a complete scene investigation; a comprehensive toxicology panel with results interpreted in the context of the circumstances of death; every responsible substance listed by generic name; deaths from misuse of opioids without apparent intent of self-harm classed as accidents, keeping 'undetermined' for the rare cases where the evidence supports more than one intent); the SAMHSA consensus panel (scene investigation, a standard of practice for forensic toxicology and guidance on documenting the cause of death, distinguishing 'drug-caused' from 'drug-detected' deaths, and noting that non-uniform classification affects the quality of incidence and prevalence data); and the Organization of Scientific Area Committees MDI subcommittee (three essential initiatives: standardized drug-related death investigation, more drug-death surveillance by medical examiners and coroners, and their access to death certificates and other information for quality control and analysis).
key_findings.locator: Investigation and Classification of Overdose Deaths › The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Relayed, not appraised; the SAMHSA panel was co-chaired by a co-author of this review (card sc_goldberger_2013).

key_findings.finding: Relayed from the first author's 2015 commentary: the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists Overdose Subcommittee advised that practitioners know the quality and limits of their jurisdiction's certificate data, check the completeness and accuracy of the codes where possible and read counts and rates with caution where the share of unspecified deaths is considerable, that jurisdictions be compared on total drug overdose death rates, and that drug-specific trends remain useful only while the degree of drug specification does not vary markedly from year to year.
key_findings.locator: Epidemiologic Analysis of Drug Overdose Death Data › Methodologic Considerations for the Analysis of ICD-10-Coded Death Certificate Data, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The same advice is a key finding of card sc_slavova_2015.

reporting_issues.issue: The review twice says about 20% of US overdose certificates name no specific drug, without a source, while it later quotes NCHS figures of 85% of certificates identifying specific drugs or drug classes in 2016 (15% without).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Identifying Specific Opioids by Cause-of-Death Text Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Death Certificates Remain the Core, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the dated NCHS series (and its 'drug or drug class' definition), not the unsourced 20%.

reporting_issues.issue: The recommendation to leave non-contributing drugs off the certificate and Gill's report that listing every drug above trace amounts is customary are placed side by side without reconciliation.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 7th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Drug-specific counts may include drugs that were present but did not contribute; the review does not estimate how often.

reporting_issues.issue: The South Carolina explanation for a doubling of the prescription-opioid death rate rests on personal correspondence, and the survey shares of offices requesting toxicology are given as 75% and '51–75%', a range for a single survey figure, without response rates; the two figures also imply that offices 'always' request testing for other opioids more often than for fentanyl and heroin, which the review leaves unexplained.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methodologic Considerations, 3rd paragraph; The MDI System and Certification of Opioid-Related Death, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Use these as illustrations; the primary sources are needed for precise figures.

reporting_issues.issue: Typographical errors: 'undermined intent' for undetermined (Methodologic Considerations, 4th paragraph); misspellings in reference annotations ('discusse', 'etimates', 'involed', 'acurate', 'commision'); and the description of Kentucky's enhanced surveillance by Hargrove et al. is cited as reference 84, an NCHS provisional-counts page, while Hargrove et al. is reference 45.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methodologic Considerations, 4th paragraph; Enhanced Drug Overdose Mortality Surveillance, 6th paragraph; references 3, 45, 49, 84, 87
